hints: Look carefully at the word growth in option B and compare it to reproduction. For a single-celled organism, what does getting bigger mean versus making a new organism?
Remember that mitosis always increases cell number by dividing one cell into two identical cells. Which option is only about a single cell getting larger, not dividing?
walkthrough:
**Recall what mitosis is for**

Think of mitosis as the copy-and-divide process. One cell divides to make two genetically identical cells.

So mitosis always increases the number of cells: $$1 \text{ cell} \rightarrow 2 \text{ identical cells}$$

**Separate growth from increase in cell number**

In multicellular organisms, growth means more cells by mitosis. But a unicellular organism is just one cell.

Its growth means that one cell gets bigger in size and mass, not that it divides into two cells.

**Pick the odd one out**

Asexual reproduction, tissue repair and replacement of dead cells all need new identical cells, so they all need mitosis.

Only growth of a unicellular organism is just cell enlargement, so it does not involve mitosis. That is B.

options.A: Asexual reproduction does involve mitosis, as it produces genetically identical offspring by cell division.
options.B: Growth of a unicellular organism is an increase in cell size and mass of that one cell, not division into two cells, so it does not involve mitosis.
options.C: Repair of tissues by cell replacement does involve mitosis to make new identical cells to fill the gap.
options.D: Replacement of damaged or dead cells does involve mitosis to produce identical replacement cells.
